title: Regression Forecast
summary: Predict what lm() prints: coefficients, predictions, R² as r², why y ~ x and x ~ y differ, the intercept-only model, and a dummy-coded group.
hints: The least-squares line always passes through (mean of x, mean of y). Here that's (3, 4).
With one predictor, R² is r². Swapping outcome and predictor changes the line, because each minimises errors in its own outcome.
A factor in `lm()` becomes a 0/1 dummy: the intercept is the reference group's mean and the coefficient is the other group's difference from it.

quiz.prompt: The least-squares line for five points:
quiz.explain: Slope b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)² = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6, and the line passes through the means (3, 4), so the intercept is 4 − 0.6 × 3 = 2.2.

quiz.code:
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
y <- c(2, 4, 5, 4, 5)
predict(lm(y ~ x), newdata = data.frame(x = 6))
quiz.explain: 2.2 + 0.6 × 6 = 5.8. (The 1 is the row name of the new data.) x = 6 is outside the data, so this is extrapolation: the line may not hold there.

quiz.code:
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
y <- c(2, 4, 5, 4, 5)
summary(lm(y ~ x))$r.squared
quiz.explain: r = .775 here, and with one predictor R² = r² = .60. The other 40% of the variance in y is in the residuals.

quiz.prompt: Swap the roles: predict x from y.
quiz.explain: Not the inverse of the first line (which would be slope 1 ÷ 0.6 = 1.67). Regressing x on y minimises errors in x, a different line. Correlation is symmetric; regression isn't, so choose the outcome on purpose.

quiz.prompt: A model with no predictor at all:
quiz.explain: With no predictor the best single prediction is the mean, 4. Its squared errors add up to SST, the yardstick R² compares the real model against.

quiz.prompt: A two-group factor as the predictor:
quiz.explain: R codes the factor as a dummy (b = 1, a = 0). The intercept is group a's mean (4) and `gb` is how much higher group b's mean is (9 − 4 = 5). Its t-test is Student's t-test: regression, t-tests and ANOVA are one model.
